---
title: "9. The market test"
aliases: [/time-series.html]
---

The model is now fully assembled, and every parameter has already been
used. The household's preferences were pinned down by consumption
moments in [Chapter 5](05-long-run-risks.qmd), and the cash-flow
loadings were measured from dividends and consumption in
[Chapter 8](08-calibrating-cash-flows.qmd). No parameter is left that
could be adjusted to match a return. The first comparison with
asset-price data is therefore an out-of-sample test. Hand the
calibrated household the calibrated aggregate dividend claim, and ask
what it pays for the claim and what it earns on the claim.

The aggregate market is where the long-run risks model family was
built to be tested (Bansal and Yaron 2004), and the test has two
targets at once. The market out-earns a Treasury bill by seven to
eight percentage points a year over 1930 to 2003, and it trades at a
mean price-dividend ratio near thirty, a valuation that swings from 10
to 88 across the sample. A DCF can hit either target alone, because it
has a free number to spend on it. The model here has no free number
left, so it is graded on both targets together. A match on the equity
premium at the wrong valuation is a fail, and so is the reverse.

One more check comes before prices. The calibrated cash-flow processes
must themselves look like the data when simulated. If simulated
consumption and dividends do not resemble the sample, a later match on
returns could come from wrong cash flows rather than from correct
pricing, and the test ends there.

## The economics of the test

Nothing new is derived here. The Euler equation
$E_t[M_{t+1} R_{i,t+1}] = 1$ with the Epstein-Zin kernel
([Chapter 4](04-epstein-zin-preferences.qmd)) prices the market claim,
and the Tauchen-Hussey solver of [Chapter 7](07-quadrature-solution.qmd)
computes the valuation function $z(x_t, \sigma_t^2)$ on a grid without
log-linear approximation. The new part is the object being compared to
the data.

The paper's Table VII reports sample statistics, not population
moments. Each entry is the average, across 1,000 artificial samples,
of a statistic estimated on 74 years of annual data. Each artificial
sample is simulated at the monthly frequency and aggregated to years,
so it has exactly the length of the 1930 to 2003 sample. The
construction matters for grading, because a 74-year sample average is
a noisy draw. The model is asked whether the data look like a typical
sample from it, and the cross-sample standard deviation says how far a
typical sample strays. `lrr.simulate_table_vii` reproduces the same
object. The page runs 300 samples rather than 1,000 to keep the build
fast, and the printed means barely move.

## Hands-on: the data targets

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
# Data bootstrap: use the repo's committed CSVs, or fetch them when this
# notebook runs outside the repository.
from pathlib import Path
import urllib.request

DATA = Path("../../data")
if not DATA.exists():
    DATA = Path("data")
    DATA.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    base = ("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tlorans/"
            "kiku-value-premium-replication/main/data/")
    for f in ("annual_panel.csv", "consumption_annual.csv", "rf_annual.csv"):
        if not (DATA / f).exists():
            urllib.request.urlretrieve(base + f, DATA / f)
```

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import lrrcs as lrr

dc = pd.read_csv(DATA / "consumption_annual.csv").sort_values("year")
panel = pd.read_csv(DATA / "annual_panel.csv")
rf = pd.read_csv(DATA / "rf_annual.csv")
y = dc["dc"].to_numpy()
mkt = panel[panel["claim"] == "Market"].merge(dc, on="year").sort_values("year")
```

```{python}
print(f"{len(mkt)} years, 1930-2003")
print(f"consumption growth : mean {y.mean()*100:.2f}%, "
      f"sd {y.std(ddof=1)*100:.2f}%, AC1 {np.corrcoef(y[:-1], y[1:])[0, 1]:.2f}")
print(f"market return      : mean {mkt['ret'].mean()*100:.2f}%, "
      f"sd {mkt['ret'].std(ddof=1)*100:.1f}%")
print(f"market dividends   : mean {mkt['dgrowth'].mean()*100:.1f}%, "
      f"sd {mkt['dgrowth'].std(ddof=1)*100:.1f}%, "
      f"corr(dc, dd) {np.corrcoef(mkt['dc'], mkt['dgrowth'])[0, 1]:.2f}")
print(f"real T-bill        : mean {rf['rf'].mean()*100:.2f}%")
print(f"market valuation   : mean P/D {mkt['pd'].mean():.1f}, "
      f"mean log P/D {np.log(mkt['pd']).mean():.2f}")
```

Read the targets off the print. Consumption growth averages 1.75
percent with a 2.37 percent standard deviation, so the endowment is
smooth. The smoothness is why a market return of 8.5 percent is a
puzzle. The first autocorrelation of 0.41 says expected growth is not
a constant. The reconstruction's real T-bill averages 0.07 percent,
while the paper's sample, on a slightly different vintage, prints 0.91
percent. The safe rate is the one series where the reconstruction and
the paper's data differ visibly, and I quote both below. The valuation
also moves a lot across the sample, as the figure below shows.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-cap: "Market log price-dividend ratio, 1930 to 2003, using Campbell-Shiller dividends on the CRSP reconstruction. The dashed line is the sample mean of 3.33. The model must produce the premium and the valuation level together."
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

log_pd = np.log(mkt["pd"].to_numpy())
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.2))
ax.plot(mkt["year"], log_pd, color="#1b1714", lw=1.3)
ax.axhline(log_pd.mean(), color="#7a1f1f", lw=1.0, ls="--")
ax.set_xlabel("year")
ax.set_ylabel("log(P/D)")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## First check: do the simulated cash flows look like the sample?

`lrr.simulate_cashflow_moments` runs the calibrated endowment forward,
using twenty artificial 74-year samples here, and reports average
annual moments:

```{python}
mom = lrr.simulate_cashflow_moments(n_sims=20, years=74, seed=1)
cons = mom["consumption"]
mdiv = mom["dividends"]["market"]
print(f"consumption      : mean {cons['E[dc]']:.2f}%, "
      f"sd {cons['sigma(dc)']:.2f}%, AC1 {cons['AC1']:.2f}")
print(f"market dividends : mean {mdiv['E[dd]']:.2f}%, "
      f"sd {mdiv['sigma(dd)']:.1f}%, corr(dc, dd) {mdiv['corr(dc,dd)']:.2f}")
```

Simulated consumption growth averages 1.82 percent with a 2.44 percent
standard deviation, against 1.75 and 2.37 in the data, so the endowment
side passes. Market dividend growth is an order of magnitude more
volatile than consumption, in the model as in the data (16.4 percent
simulated against the 11.0 percent the data cell printed; the note
below explains the gap). Its correlation with consumption growth is
0.57 simulated against 0.60 in the data. The autocorrelation print and
the dividend volatility print need a comment before anyone reads them
as failures.

::: {.callout-warning title="Two annualization conventions affect this print"}
The cell prints a first autocorrelation of simulated annual consumption
growth of 0.16, while the data show 0.41 and my Table III reports 0.43
for the model. The gap comes from the measurement convention, not from
the economics. The paper aggregates simulated monthly data the way
NIPA, the national income and product accounts, builds annual
consumption. It sums the twelve monthly levels within the year, then
takes log growth of the annual sums. Aggregating levels in that way
smooths the annual series, so it raises the autocorrelation and damps
the year-over-year volatility (Working 1960). The helper here sums the
twelve monthly log growth rates instead, which does neither. The same
convention gap accounts for a good part of the dividend volatility
print of 16.4 against the data's 11.0. The economy is the same, and
the two annualization conventions produce different annual prints. The
persistence the pricing relies on sits in the monthly state $x_t$
under either convention.
:::

The check passes. The endowment's mean and volatility and the
correlation between consumption and dividend growth land near the
sample, and the two visible gaps come from the annualization
convention rather than from the calibration. Prices come next.

## Second check: solve, simulate, and grade both targets

Solve the model on the paper's grid of 30 points for $x$ and 4 for
$\sigma^2$, which [Chapter 7](07-quadrature-solution.qmd) built. Then
generate 300 samples of 74 years and average the sample statistics,
exactly as the data column was constructed:

```{python}
params = lrr.get_table_ii_params()
solver = lrr.ModelSolver(params, n_x=30, n_s=4).solve()
tab = lrr.simulate_table_vii(solver, n_samples=300, years=74, seed=0)
```

```{python}
print(f"risk-free rate    : {tab['mean_rf']:5.2f}%  (SE {tab['mean_rf_se']:.2f})")
print(f"market return     : {tab['mean_return']['market']:5.2f}%  "
      f"(SE {tab['mean_return_se']['market']:.2f})")
print(f"equity premium    : {tab['mean_return']['market'] - tab['mean_rf']:5.2f}%")
print(f"return volatility : {tab['volatility']['market']:5.2f}%")
print(f"mean log P/D      : {tab['mean_log_pd']['market']:5.2f}")
```

The table below places the page's model prints next to the paper's
own prints. The paper's Table VII uses 1,000 samples and a slightly
different data vintage, and the SE columns are cross-sample standard
deviations.

|  | Model (this page) | Model (paper prints) | Data (reconstruction) | Data (paper prints) |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Market return, % | 8.93 (3.25) | 7.53 (2.69) | 8.52 | 8.56 (1.79) |
| Return volatility, % | 19.68 | not reported | 20.1 | 20.1 |
| Risk-free rate, % | 1.04 (0.62) | 1.58 | 0.07 | 0.91 (0.39) |
| Mean log P/D | 3.01 | 3.24 | 3.33 | 3.34 (0.13) |

Grade both targets. The model earns 8.93 percent on the market claim
against 8.52 in the data, which is an equity premium of 7.89 percent
over its own safe rate, against 7.65 on the paper's data prints (8.56
minus 0.91). Return volatility is 19.68 percent against 20.1. The
valuation comes out at a mean log price-dividend ratio of 3.01 against
3.33, so the model matches the premium at close to the data's
valuation level. The safe rate lands at 1.04 percent, between the
reconstruction's 0.07 and the paper's model print of 1.58. My own
prints differ from the cells on the page by less than one cross-sample
standard deviation. The run here uses 300 samples, a 30-point grid,
and one seed, and [Chapter 10](10-value-premium-resolved.qmd)
quantifies how the grid moves the numbers. The verdict does not move.
Both targets land, and no return entered the calibration.

The contrast with a DCF is the point of the test. A DCF matching the
8.5 percent return would have assumed a discount rate near 8.5, and a
DCF matching the valuation would have assumed the growth number. Here,
consumption moments fixed the household, and dividends fixed the
claim. The Euler equation then produced the premium, the volatility,
and the valuation together. The market test is passed, but matching
the market does not rank firms. The cross-section is the next chapter.

## Takeaways

- Nothing was left to tune. Preferences came from consumption, and
  cash flows came from dividends, so the market row is out of sample
  and the model is graded on the premium and the valuation together.
- Simulated cash flows pass their own check first (consumption mean
  1.82 vs 1.75, sd 2.44 vs 2.37). The printed AC1 of 0.16 comes from
  the annualization convention, not from a persistence failure.
- The solved model prints a market return of 8.93 percent (data: 8.52),
  volatility of 19.68 (data: 20.1), a safe rate of 1.04, and a mean log
  P/D of 3.01 (data: 3.33). Both targets land, and the safe rate and
  the exact valuation are sensitive to the grid.
- Table VII is a sampling object. It reports means over hundreds of
  74-year samples, with cross-sample dispersion, which is the right way
  to compare a model to one 74-year history.

   the market return and the safe rate move? Compare the movement to
   the printed SE columns.
